title: Doubt
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna's main teaching is that doubt can be both beneficial and harmful in the context of meditation practice, but ultimately serves as a catalyst for growth and awakening. By embracing great doubt and questioning our current understanding, we can tear down old certainties and find new insights, allowing us to approach challenges with a fresh perspective and deepen our practice over time. This process requires courage, humility, and openness, and is essential for manifesting Buddha nature and realizing our true potential.

sentences.text: **Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna:** Well, thanks everybody for being here.
I want to welcome Tim back from his travels, and I also want to wish Bob good health and a fast recovery.
I know some of you had intended to be out there tonight, so hopefully next year we'll be able to sit in the Cedar Grove again.
I spent quite a bit of time this past year working on the kalesas myself.
Kalesa, first of all, is a Pali term for poisons or defilements.
These are mental or emotional states, and they cloud the mind and create obstacles to practice.
They can be mental, they can be emotional, so just as they say, they're poisons or defilements.
The Buddha spoke about five hindrances specifically to practice, and I'll just review those.
Most of you are probably pretty familiar with them, and some of you aren't.
Just real fast.
First one is greed or desire, and the second one is aversion or ill will and extreme hatred.
The third one they call sloth and torpor, which are kind of funny words, so you can interpret that as laziness or inertia or dullness.
Then there's restlessness and worry, and the last one is doubt.
In the Pali Canon, these were traditionally taught as impediments to meditation practice, but we can also apply them to our everyday life, life in general.
The one I want to talk about tonight is doubt, and I sort of came by this unexpectedly.
A few weeks ago anyway, I got up early in the morning and I just started writing.
I had written about, I don't know, eight pages or whatever, and when I went back and looked at it, I thought, this is about doubt.
It's something I had sort of overlooked when I was going through the rest of the obstacles, and so I guess I need to study this.
What you're hearing are my reflections and then a couple of words from some other people too.
Doubt can be both beneficial and harmful, first of all.
First I'm going to tackle the debilitating side effects of doubt.
I've read that it's often the greatest block to our spiritual understanding, even more so than greed or aversion, as it tends to ignite all the other ones.
If there's doubt happening, then that's going to infuse any other hindrance that you're working with probably, and that may be where it starts.
It can result in indecisiveness, a lack of focus, and general confusion, all of which lead to an inability to really commit and to probe any particular path over time and with some determination.
I think we would all be aware of this: it really does take time and determination to understand anything that we're going to study at all.

If we dabble and we wander around from interest to interest, buffeted around by our likes and dislikes, we will probably accumulate a lot of information maybe, but we won't really understand anything with real depth.
Over time, doubt can diminish our confidence in ourselves and our capacities, and our trust in the practice and even in the world around us.
At its worst, our confusion can lead to paralysis and depression.
So doubt has these emotional effects, and it also has cognitive effects.
It can really begin to tyrannize our thinking.
Because this hindering doubt is often characterized by strong opinions and judgments, it tends towards what I'm calling overgeneralizing.

For instance, if we're having difficulty with something in our daily life or our practice, doubt can translate these experiences into broad and vague statements and ways of interpreting the experience.
I'll use my job as an example.
I work with young people in the high school with behavioral disabilities and developmental disabilities.
I might be having a hard time someday with a student, which happens frequently, and I could describe the situation just as it happened and say, "I had difficulties with a student yesterday.
He lost his temper and it just took me hours to get him back on track."
Or I might generalize and say, "I really suck at this job.
And these kids are never going to get it right."
I might say that about them.
I could put it on myself and say that I'm doing a lousy job, or I just might say, "These kids are hopeless.
And my staff is hopeless.
Nobody came to help me."

If I continue to think this way, eventually I'd start identifying myself and others with these all-or-nothing stories, which eventually grow into life stories that are disempowering for ourselves and for other people we're projecting them on.
These stories prevent us from gaining any insight into our problems and their solutions, and from recognizing our own real, actual limitations and capabilities.
Then they just create more confusion, and things begin to cycle around and around.
So I certainly have plenty of opportunities to watch my own stories that have grown out of self-doubt.
I have also learned about this doubt that is characterized by comparison.
Really the whole construction of self is based on comparison when you start to think about it.
But with this doubt, there's in a sense a social yardstick, I've called it, applied to and interfering with, really obstructing, all relationships.

When we are in a relationship with a person, or perhaps we meet somebody at a party or wherever, there's this maybe subliminal, maybe more conscious thing that happens where we're measuring ourselves up with this person.
What's this person better at than I am?
Am I less than this person, more than this person?
Maybe we're the same, and generally we think we're the same, and maybe we get along really well.
But this doubt, based on that, begins and ends in separation as opposed to intimacy with this other person.
So it can be really pretty destructive in that way.
Now, if we look at practice, how might that be affected by doubt?
Well, in our tradition, in the Mahayana teachings, there is this understanding of Buddha nature, as we call it.
In Shambhala, I know they call it basic goodness, which is a nice, simple definition for it.
This is a very foundational teaching about our essential wholeness and our clarity of heart and mind.

With this principle as a basis, we can go forward with some lightness of heart, I would call it that, that allows us both to live our stories as we do and will, and also to go beyond them at the same time.
However, there is violence and corruption in the world, and it can make us skeptical of this basic goodness and can even lead to cynicism.
That's looking outward.
When we look in at ourselves, at our own ignorance and mishaps, we can easily begin to doubt our own capacities to manifest this Buddha nature, and then we lose sight of this vast potential.
Of course, this toxic doubt transfers to our time on the cushion.

Even though we understand the simplicity of the method of zazen, for example, returning again and again to this presence of life in ourselves, our self-doubt confuses us and tells us that we're not doing it right, leading to more constriction and frustration.
We begin to see practice as a laborious self-improvement project, measuring our progress and our failures.
Once again, we start to compare.
It's like, "Oh man, they all know the forms, and I'm going counterclockwise, and they're going clockwise," or "I only rang the bell once, and I was supposed to ring the bell twice."
We all know this stuff.
This is the comparison again.
Now, I grew up as a Catholic, and when thinking about doubt, what came to mind for me is St.
John of the Cross, who talked about the dark night of the soul.
There are different ways of interpreting this, and I'll express really only one of them.
This is a period of searing and excruciating doubt, which can last for many years.
I think all of us here are probably familiar with Mother Teresa, and you probably know that she went through this for 50 years and continued to work as she did.
The way she described it was that she felt no presence of God whatsoever.
This is not specific to Christian mystics.
I read a bit about what Jack Kornfield had to say about this.
There are a couple of other practitioners from our own Zen tradition as well, but in our tradition this was described more as a dry spell, devoid of the aspiration to wake up.
Kornfield says it often appears after the student has been practicing for a number of years and has had some spiritual openings.
But then, like everything, these heightened states come, and then they pass away and they change.
The practitioner's early fantasies and expectations, like "I'm going to be enlightened tomorrow" or "I'm going to be totally serene and my life is going to be totally sweet," well, those are not met.
This stage, he says, can touch some very painful and overwhelming places, and the student drops the practice altogether.
However, if the student finds support in a teacher and a community, she can integrate this dark night into practice and emerge from that with joy and equanimity.
Joan Halifax is a person who described her own suffering through this dark night.
I actually listened to her speak about this.
It happened during the time that she was initially setting up by a Zen center, and she was reluctant to go through it, wondering whether she had the strength to go through it.
But she uses the analogy of her Sonicare toothbrush to describe her process of the dark night, so I'm going to give you my own iteration of her Sonicare toothbrush story.
She loved her Sonicare toothbrush and was really excited to have one in the beginning.
She was so excited about it that she brushed her teeth four or five times a day, thinking about the prospects of her cavity-free, dazzling white mouth.
But eventually the enthusiasm wore off, there were no more thrills, and five times a day grew to four, then three, then two.
Her good sense told her she shouldn't stop, and even though the thrill was gone, she just sailed it on, brushing away day to day, doing what was in front of her.
I don't know, it's not really funny, it's right there.
Anyway, she grew content in her practice.
She was at ease and her teeth were happy.
So in the end, what she did was really disavow her preferences.

She continued to follow the teachings and put one foot in front of the other, and she didn't buy into the stories that she was wrong, or her teachers were wrong, or that the practice or life was wrong.

She went through this for three years, of heaviness, and she confirmed what Thomas Merton had to say about this dry spot or this dark night, and these are Thomas Merton's words: "True love and prayer are learned in the moment when prayer has become impossible and the heart has turned to stone."
Then she herself, I have a quote from her about this too, says, "Catastrophe is the essence of the spiritual path.
A series of breakdowns allowing us to discover the threads that weave all of life into a whole cloth."
So we may not necessarily reach extremes like this, but we can use our very doubt in profitable ways to doubt our own doubt.
We can question the reality of our stories like she did.
We can challenge the tactics we use to run away from our own pain and our own confusion, and we probably know all those.
Blaming, of course, is one.
We might overwork or overeat or over browse or Facebook or whatever it is we do to avoid ourselves and to avoid life.
In fact, we may even misuse our own spiritual teachings to simply create a stronger identity on the path.
So we can begin to watch all of those things.
Once we've examined all of that, we can sit.

We can just sit with our uncertainties and allow our doubts and demons in viscerally, with great tenderness and loving kindness, remembering that all beings suffer like this and that we are in concert with them.
If we can do this, we'll find the other side of doubt: this doubt that doubts doubt and uses it as a doorway to the unknown.
Then our doubt, which used to be a hindrance, is now transformed and this becomes our great doubt.
This is what gives fuel and vitality to our practice.
Now, what is great doubt?
We talk about it, and I didn't find any good definition for it, so you're going to get mine.
This is a doubt that grows out of a willingness and a hunger, as I see it, to really penetrate the mysteries of life, of death, of self, and just about everything in between.
It can also be uncomfortable, just the same way a doubt that is a hindrance can be.
We have to get out of our base of knowledge that we've grown up with, that we've been educated with, that we've been totally inculcated with.
But we do have our own natural wonder, if we go back to our days of childhood when we all had this sense of play and wonder and our curiosity.
And we also have our [unclear: "great sorrow rules"] to spur us on in pursuing this great doubt.
So our job here with great doubt, as I see it, is to simply abide in the questions without clinging to the answers, and just let the questions open us up and reveal themselves.
I have a little bit of a story related to great doubt.
I was at a friend's house a few weeks ago, and we were watching her toddler, Quinn.

Quinn was tossing some balls around, just playing while she and I were sitting there talking, and he was so absolutely delighted at how this basketball would roll back and forth and come back to him, and how he would be slamming it against the wall and hearing it.
Oh, the noise was great, and how it stopped the conversation in the room.
He really liked it when he stopped talking.
Then he watched how it would go around the corner and disappear and just go out of sight, and he also liked to watch how it intimidated the cat.
The cat would run away and go crazy.
He went really off and on with this ball and some other ones for two hours, this kid, quietly.
It was incredible.
He was totally absorbed in it.
My friend and I talked, and we watched, ultimately.
I thought, now this is great doubt, [unclear: "the con of the basketball"].
As I see it, our Zen tradition really nourishes and encourages this spirit of inquiry.
To see this explicitly practiced, expressed in practice, we have Koan study.
I think this is a manifestation of the spirit of inquiry that we have.
And Hakuin, who I read a bit about, who has a [unclear: "pretty fascinating cat"], who was the 18th century Rinzai teacher, said, "At the bottom of great doubt lies great awakening.
If you doubt fully, you will awaken fully."
Hakuin developed this systemized practice of Koan study, a curriculum, with repeated testing.
You go into the room, and then you get dinged out because you probably got it wrong, and you can go through that for years and years.
His practice was extremely arduous.
He was one of these guys that'd sit there and clench his teeth, and [unclear: "didn't really work at it"].
But he was also known to have experienced what we would probably call today a mental breakdown, as a result of the rigor that he applied to his practice.
He spent two years in rehab, so to speak.
He went off with a Taoist hermit from the mountains and learned some breathing techniques and other stuff from this hermit fellow, and eventually got over it and returned to his practice.
I have to say, I'm not particularly a big fan of this type of practice, and I am really happy to be here where we offer a gentler way through our [unclear: "sodas"] and practice.
Which isn't to say that Dogen's way doesn't have its own challenges and frustrations.
Dogen's talks and his writings are also Koans in themselves.
They're paradoxical, beautifully poetic, filled with metaphors and images from his day.
But we have a tendency, I think, to tease them, to tweeze them out gently.
We chant them, particularly on Saturday morning, when we do the [unclear: "Bukan Zazengi"] and the Genjokoan, and we chant that over and over again, and we have talks on them, and we reflect.
By just sitting, until they grow into us over time, I feel like that's sort of like a graft to a tree.
The questions emerge, and certain phrases of his or other ones from the chants will grab hold of us, and the responses over time morph and deepen in really unexpected circumstances and places.
I think we've all probably experienced this over time with our practice.
Unlike Quinn's basketball, however, our Koans aren't always so playful.
They are the Koans of our everyday life.
Everyday life is our way and lineage.
Suzuki Roshi said, "Enlightened is not any particular stage that you attain.
When you understand your life completely, that is enlightened."
So sometimes the teachings of our life might be painful, but with time and practice, we approach them like the basketball.
Watch how they go up and down, slam up against the wall, then go around the corner and disappear, only to reappear again.
I'm going to cut myself off, actually, because I really do want to have a little go around the circle.
Before I do that, I had pretty much put the talk away and let it go for a while, and I got onto the Everyday Zen site, which I do periodically.
On the home page of Norman's site was a quote by Norman.
I want to go around the circle, but I want you to be thinking of this quote.
I was going to copy it and pass it around to you so you could really look at it, but now you'll just have to remember, because this is a test.
So here's what he says.
*It's necessary to keep things honest.
In order to have some faith, you absolutely have to doubt.
You have to wonder whether yesterday's truth still applies today.
You have to ask if it does or not.
Be willing to tear down today's truth to find something, if anything, behind it.
This makes life and religion alive.*
You want me to read it one more time?
Okay.
*It's necessary to keep things honest.
In order to have some faith, you absolutely have to have doubt.
You have to wonder whether yesterday's truth still applies today.
You have to ask if it does or not.
Be willing to tear down today's truth to find something, if anything, behind it.
This makes life and religion alive.*
So you don't really have to respond to that.
I'm just throwing it out there.
I'm sure all of us, I mean these hindrances and places, they're universal.
I'm sure we have all had doubts in different ways, and maybe they're great doubts, and maybe they're small doubts.
So whatever comes up, and again, if you don't wish to speak, just bow and pass, that's fine.
Well, why don't we, we won't put Nick on the spot.
We'll put Tim on the spot first, and we'll go around the circle that way.
**Participant:** What?
I actually don't understand what you want us to say.
**Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna:** Oh, well, anything you want about doubt, first of all.
That's why I read Norman's quote, thinking that we could respond, if you chose to respond, to that particular quote.
And if you have had doubts of your own, great doubt or small doubts.
That's a little broad, but go for it.
**Participant:** Well, there may be about, like, I'm going to make something happen, kind of forced.
